summary:
The Sphery Project helps anyone, irrespective of field, look at, understand and personally use official data from the NASA SPHEREx satellite. It's divided into two parts: the Dome view and the Pro view. The Dome view drops you into a grassy field under a dome that simulates the night sky in optical, near-infrared, and mid-infrared views. Click any point to take it to the Pro view, where you can explore the details. The Pro view is a dashboard for the selected point. You can search the IRSA archive by object name or position, open real SPHEREx FITS images, and compare the six detector bands. You can also measure brightness and identify the object.

details:
The problem

SPHEREx is mapping the whole sky in infrared, and its data is public, but most professional astronomy software looks like an aircraft control panel. A student who is interested in astronomy and wants to get into the field opens one of these tools, sees hundreds of buttons and gives up before they ever see a real image. The Sphery Project is made for those students. It lets anyone look at, understand and personally use official data from the NASA SPHEREx sattelite without learning a whole professional tool first.

What it does

The user starts in the dome and clicks any patch of sky that interests them. They then take that exact point to the Pro view to find out more about it. A landing page comes before both of these and explains the satellite itself.

The three parts

Landing page - has general information about the project and the SPHEREx satellite. It includes a 3D model of the satellite that we made with GLM 5.3 (the shapes are approximate). It lets the user explore how the satellite works, how one exposure becomes six pictures and a full spectrum, the mission timeline and what each part does in high detail.

Dome view – puts the user in the centre of a grass field covered by a dome that simulates the night sky. The sky can be switched between optical (DSS2), near-infrared (2MASS) and mid-infrared (AllWISE) views. Clicking any point shows its coordinates and how many SPHEREx frames are nearby. You can also type an object name like M42 or Sirius and go straight to it.

Pro view is a dashboard for the point you clicked. You can search the IRSA archive by object name or position in the sky and open the real SPHEREx FITS images. FITS is the standard image format astronomers use; it stores the pixel values and a header that describes them. You can blink between the six detector bands to compare the same spot at different wavelengths. You can also measure how bright something is with aperture photometry (the total light inside a small circle with the background taken out) and see which catalogued object is actually sitting there.

Try it.

Open the link and look around the dome.

Switch the sky layers and click a point, or type an object name like M42.

Press “Investigate this region”.

In the Pro view, search an object like M31 or Orion, open an image, compare the bands and measure the brightness.

What is real, and what is simulated?

We want to be clear about this. The Dome sky is survey imagery (DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE); it is not SPHEREx data. The Dome observer is simulated at latitude 30° S at a fixed moment, so it is not the user's location or the live sky. “Frames nearby” counts frame centres close to the point, not exact coverage. The 3D spacecraft, the orbit position and the clouds on Earth are illustrative, not live. The real SPHEREx data only appears in the Pro view.

Who it helps

Mainly students who are interested in astronomy and want to help in the field but are put off because the professional software looks so complicated. The Dome gives them an easy way in, and the Pro view lets them touch real data the same way a professional does.

Limits and setbacks

The traffic limit is 2,500 people, so the app can only handle that many users at a time.

The Dome fell below our expectations because we ran out of time. The sky is soft when you zoom in, so the Dome is for finding your way around, and the detail is in the Pro view.

The data comes from older NASA data and is not updated live. Updating it is hard because the backend is heavy and slow to work with, and this was a real pain for us during the hackathon.

Tools

JavaScript, Three.js, Python (numpy, astropy, scipy) and GLM 5.3 for the 3D model.
